title: A Clock You Can Transplant, and How Light Sets It

scenes.visual: Title card: A Clock You Can Transplant, and How Light Sets It.

scenes.tts: Destroy one tiny pair of nuclei above the optic chiasm, and a rat's daily rhythms of drinking and running vanish. Is that a clock, or a relay?
scenes.visual: A rat actogram: rows of daily activity bands line up neatly. After a lesion mark, the bands dissolve into scattered activity. On-screen question: clock or relay?
scenes.narration: Destroy one tiny pair of nuclei above the optic chiasm, and a rat's daily rhythms of drinking and running vanish. Is that a clock, or a relay?

scenes.tts: The rats still drank, but not on a daily schedule. Yet a lesion also cuts passing fibres, so it cannot tell a clock from a relay.
scenes.visual: Drinking marks: nightly clusters before the lesion, scattered after. Label: Stephan and Zucker, 1972. Fibres through the lesion site are cut and the lesioned region is crossed out. Two open boxes, clock and relay, joined by: a lesion alone cannot tell.
scenes.narration: The rats still drank, but not on a daily schedule. Yet a lesion also cuts passing fibres, so it cannot tell a clock from a relay.

scenes.tts: In hamsters, a mutation called tau makes the clock run fast, which labels whose clock is running.
scenes.visual: Two hamster actograms: wild-type rows stacked straight; tau/tau rows slope, each day starting earlier. Period values on screen only: wild type about 24 h, tau/tau about 20 h.
scenes.narration: In hamsters, a mutation called tau makes the clock run fast, which labels whose clock is running.

scenes.tts: Destroy a host's supra-kye-az-matic nucleus, or S C N. Then graft in S C N tissue from a donor of a different genotype. Whose period comes back?
scenes.visual: Host hamster with a lesioned SCN; its actogram shows activity scattered across all clock times, with no daily band. Label: activity persists, rhythm gone. A graft arrow from a donor hamster. On-screen question: whose period?
scenes.narration: Destroy a host's suprachiasmatic nucleus, or SCN. Then graft in SCN tissue from a donor of a different genotype. Whose period comes back?
scenes.caption: Destroy a host's suprachiasmatic nucleus, or SCN. Then graft in SCN tissue from a donor of a different genotype. Whose period comes back?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; a small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: The donor's, whatever the host's genotype. A relay would pass on the host's timing. A clock imposes its own.
scenes.visual: The host's actogram returns, its rows sloping at the donor's period. Label: Ralph and colleagues, 1990: donor's period.
scenes.narration: The donor's, whatever the host's genotype. A relay would pass on the host's timing. A clock imposes its own.

scenes.tts: How does a cell keep time? Two proteins, clock and bee-mal one, pair up and switch on the genes for per and cry.
scenes.caption: How does a cell keep time? Two proteins, CLOCK and BMAL1, pair up and switch on the genes for PER and CRY.
scenes.visual: A nucleus cartoon: CLOCK and BMAL1 bound as a pair on a DNA strip labelled E-box; Per and Cry genes light up.
scenes.narration: How does a cell keep time? Two proteins, CLOCK and BMAL1, pair up and switch on the genes for PER and CRY.

scenes.tts: Per and cry proteins build up, bind each other, and enter the nucleus.
scenes.caption: PER and CRY proteins build up, bind each other, and enter the nucleus.
scenes.visual: PER and CRY proteins accumulate in the cytoplasm, pair up and move through the nuclear envelope.
scenes.narration: PER and CRY proteins build up, bind each other, and enter the nucleus.

scenes.tts: There they stop clock and bee-mal one, so per and cry switch off their own genes. That is the brake.
scenes.caption: There they stop CLOCK and BMAL1, so PER and CRY switch off their own genes. That is the brake.
scenes.visual: PER-CRY sits on CLOCK-BMAL1, labelled brake; the Per and Cry genes go dark.
scenes.narration: There they stop CLOCK and BMAL1, so PER and CRY switch off their own genes. That is the brake.

scenes.tts: Only as per and cry are broken down does the brake come off. Then a new cycle begins.
scenes.caption: Only as PER and CRY are broken down does the brake come off. Then a new cycle begins.
scenes.visual: PER-CRY fragments and fades; CLOCK-BMAL1 lights the genes again. A circular arrow labelled about 24 h.
scenes.narration: Only as PER and CRY are broken down does the brake come off. Then a new cycle begins.

scenes.tts: Why does it cycle, instead of settling? Think of a shower with a long pipe.
scenes.visual: A shower with a long coiled pipe between the tap and the head.
scenes.narration: Why does it cycle, instead of settling? Think of a shower with a long pipe.

scenes.tts: You turn toward hot, and nothing changes. You turn further. When the hot water arrives, you have overshot.
scenes.visual: A hand turns the tap; the water stays blue, then arrives red. A temperature trace overshoots, then swings back past the target.
scenes.narration: You turn toward hot, and nothing changes. You turn further. When the hot water arrives, you have overshot.

scenes.tts: Feedback that is delayed enough, and strong enough, keeps overshooting. In the clock, these steps together set a cycle of about a day.
scenes.visual: The temperature trace keeps swinging and morphs into a PER level trace across days. Labels for the steps: transcription, translation, modification, nuclear entry, degradation, plus steep repression.
scenes.narration: Feedback that is delayed enough, and strong enough, keeps overshooting. In the clock, these steps together set a cycle of about a day.

scenes.tts: About a day, not exactly. So light resets it each day.
scenes.visual: Text on screen: near 24 h, not exactly 24. A sun icon nudges the clock.
scenes.narration: About a day, not exactly. So light resets it each day.

scenes.tts: Some retinal ganglion cells sense light themselves, using a pigment called melanopsin. Their axons reach the clock through the retinohypothalamic tract.
scenes.visual: An eye in cross-section; a few ganglion cells glow, labelled melanopsin. Their axons run to the SCN, labelled retinohypothalamic tract. Rods and cones glow faintly too.
scenes.narration: Some retinal ganglion cells sense light themselves, using a pigment called melanopsin. Their axons reach the clock through the retinohypothalamic tract.

scenes.tts: When the light arrives matters. Light in your biological evening says the day is not over yet. The clock runs later.
scenes.visual: A day-night bar labelled example: habitual sleep 00:00 to 08:00, temperature low near 06:00. A light burst at 23:00, before the low; an arrow pushes the clock marker later. Label: phase delay.
scenes.narration: When the light arrives matters. Light in your biological evening says the day is not over yet. The clock runs later.

scenes.tts: Light in your biological morning says the day began early. Which way does that move the clock?
scenes.visual: A light burst at 07:00 on the same bar, after the temperature low, with the sleeper already up. On-screen question: earlier or later?
scenes.narration: Light in your biological morning says the day began early. Which way does that move the clock?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; a small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: Earlier. The switchover falls near the daily low of body temperature, in the early morning hours.
scenes.visual: An arrow pushes the marker earlier, labelled phase advance. A body-temperature curve below, its low point marking the switchover.
scenes.narration: Earlier. The switchover falls near the daily low of body temperature, in the early morning hours.

scenes.tts: In one study, the human clock averaged a little longer than a day. For a clock like that, the morning advance must outweigh the evening delay.
scenes.visual: On screen only: study mean period 24.18 h, idealized example; needs about 10.8 min of net advance per day. A morning arrow slightly longer than an evening arrow.
scenes.narration: In one study, the human clock averaged a little longer than a day. For a clock like that, the morning advance must outweigh the evening delay.

scenes.tts: Keep this. The S C N imposes its own period. A gene loop keeps its time. Daily light keeps it on the day.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card with three small icons: graft, loop, sun.
scenes.narration: Keep this. The SCN imposes its own period. A gene loop keeps its time. Daily light keeps it on the day.
scenes.caption: Keep this. The SCN imposes its own period. A gene loop keeps its time. Daily light keeps it on the day.
